title: Use components, state, and types
outcome: Build an interactive typed component and explain what state controls.
story: The shop interface is growing. Amina wants reusable pieces that stay in step with their data, and the team wants help catching inconsistent field names before running the app.

frames.explanation: A React component describes what to show from its current state.

values.label: result
values.value: type error in the project check

frames.explanation: TypeScript can catch a mismatch before the app runs, when you run its type checker.

sections.title: A component describes one piece of a page
paragraphs: A React component is a function that describes an interface. JSX lets that description look like markup inside JavaScript. A component can be reused and can receive inputs called props.

In this exercise, App is the component rendered in the preview. The import brings in React, and export default makes App the component the project uses. The browser runner compiles JSX before rendering the real React interface.

sections.title: State belongs to the component
paragraphs: React.useState starts a state value and returns a function for updating it. const [messages, setMessages] = React.useState<number>(10) starts the count at 10. Calling setMessages tells React to render using a new value.

For an update based on the previous value, use setMessages(previous => previous + 1). This keeps repeated updates based on the latest state. Change the state rather than manually changing an unrelated DOM element.

sections.title: Types describe expectations
paragraphs: TypeScript adds type information to JavaScript. The annotation number describes the expected kind of value. A type checker can catch mistakes such as treating a number as a message record or using a field that does not exist.

Types do not validate data arriving from a network at runtime. Keep the validation from lesson 11. The browser preview checks behaviour and strips type annotations; run npm run typecheck in the project to get actual TypeScript diagnostics.

sections.title: Keep the boundary clear
paragraphs: The component owns its visual state, while a pricing or order function owns its business rule. Props can pass information to a smaller component without making it read arbitrary global state.

Test the behaviour a person sees: adding a message, answering one, resetting, and trying to answer below zero. The project extends this component into the inbox you already built, while retaining accessibility and error states.

exercise.title: A typed inbox counter
exercise.brief: Use the supplied React import and default App component. Build a counter that adds, answers, and resets messages. Answering below zero must keep the count at zero.
exercise.starter:
import React from "react";
export default function App() { return <main />; }

steps.title: Describe the initial interface
steps.task: Render an h1 saying Amina’s inbox, an output with id count showing 10, and an Add 1 message button.
steps.hint: Begin with the markup in the example, before adding state.

steps.title: Connect state to the action
steps.task: Use useState<number>(10). Render the state in output and update it with the Add button.
steps.hint: Use setMessages(previous => previous + 1) in an onClick handler.

steps.title: Answer safely and reset
steps.task: Add Answer 1 message and Start again buttons. Keep the count non-negative and reset it to 10.
steps.hint: Use Math.max(0, previous - 1) for answering. Reset with setMessages(10).

cases.label: A clear component heading
cases.why: The rendered component still needs meaningful structure.

cases.label: The initial state is visible
cases.why: The initial interface should reflect the initial state.

cases.label: Adding changes the visible state
cases.script: const button=[...document.querySelectorAll("button")].find(button=>button.textContent==="Add 1 message"); button.click(); await new Promise(resolve=>requestAnimationFrame(()=>requestAnimationFrame(resolve))); return document.getElementById("count").textContent;
cases.why: A real state update must change the rendered output.

cases.label: Answering decreases the state
cases.script: const button=[...document.querySelectorAll("button")].find(button=>button.textContent==="Answer 1 message"); button.click(); await new Promise(resolve=>requestAnimationFrame(()=>requestAnimationFrame(resolve))); return document.getElementById("count").textContent;
cases.why: The same state owns both kinds of update.

cases.label: Reset returns to the stated initial value
cases.script: const buttons=[...document.querySelectorAll("button")]; buttons.find(button=>button.textContent==="Add 1 message").click(); await new Promise(resolve=>requestAnimationFrame(resolve)); buttons.find(button=>button.textContent==="Start again").click(); await new Promise(resolve=>requestAnimationFrame(()=>requestAnimationFrame(resolve))); return document.getElementById("count").textContent;
cases.why: Reset should use the documented initial value.

cases.label: Answering cannot make the count negative
cases.script: const button=[...document.querySelectorAll("button")].find(button=>button.textContent==="Answer 1 message"); for(let i=0;i<15;i++)button.click(); await new Promise(resolve=>requestAnimationFrame(()=>requestAnimationFrame(resolve))); return document.getElementById("count").textContent;
cases.why: A boundary rule should hold across repeated updates.

project.title: A typed React inbox
project.brief: Rebuild the message inbox as components. Keep the business rules separate, validate external data, and run the TypeScript project check as well as the behaviour checks.
deliverables: An inbox component and a message component.
